clinicalPearls: Reactions range from expected local pain and swelling, through large local reactions, to systemic allergic reactions and anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis presents with urticaria, angio-oedema, bronchospasm, hypotension or gastrointestinal symptoms soon after the sting
Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment for systemic anaphylaxis
Massive numbers of stings can cause a toxic reaction with haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis and organ injury independent of allergy
Patients with systemic reactions should be assessed for venom-specific immunotherapy and provided with an adrenaline auto-injector
A large local reaction, though alarming, does not by itself predict future anaphylaxis
reference.pathophysiology: Hymenoptera stings inject venom containing vasoactive and enzymatic components that cause immediate local pain and inflammation. In sensitised individuals, venom-specific IgE triggers mast-cell and basophil degranulation, producing systemic allergic reactions and anaphylaxis. With very large numbers of simultaneous stings, the direct toxic load of venom can cause haemolysis, muscle breakdown and multi-organ effects even without allergy. Underlying mast-cell disorders can predispose to severe reactions.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on the sting and reaction pattern
Serum tryptase where anaphylaxis or a mast-cell disorder is suspected
Venom-specific IgE testing to guide immunotherapy after systemic reactions
Renal function and creatine kinase after massive envenomation
redFlags: Signs of haemolysis or rhabdomyolysis after many stings
Stings in a patient with known mast-cell disease
reference.prognosis: Most reactions are self-limiting, and even anaphylaxis usually responds well to prompt adrenaline; venom immunotherapy substantially reduces the risk of future severe reactions.
pitfalls: Delaying adrenaline in anaphylaxis in favour of antihistamines or steroids
Assuming a large local reaction implies high anaphylaxis risk
Missing toxic multi-organ effects after mass envenomation
Failing to refer systemic reactors for immunotherapy and provide an auto-injector
management: Treat systemic anaphylaxis immediately with intramuscular adrenaline as first-line therapy, repeated as required, alongside airway support and supine positioning with the legs raised
Give adjunctive antihistamines, corticosteroids and inhaled bronchodilators for bronchospasm, without allowing these to delay adrenaline
Manage large local reactions with cold compresses, oral analgesia, antihistamines and a short oral corticosteroid course, and remove any retained sting apparatus
In massive envenomation provide aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and monitor for haemolysis, rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury with supportive organ care
Observe patients after a systemic reaction for biphasic anaphylaxis before discharge
Prescribe an adrenaline auto-injector with a personalised action plan and training for all systemic reactors
Refer systemic reactors to an allergy service for venom-specific IgE testing and venom immunotherapy, and check serum tryptase to exclude an underlying mast-cell disorder
